title: Why Most Difficult Students Just Need Good Classroom Management classroom-management/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin critiques the common tendency among teachers to fixate on individualized interventions—contracts, incentive systems, escalating consequences—for their most difficult students while letting minor misbehavior from the rest of the class slide. He argues this selective enforcement is 'lighter fluid' for difficult students, since it reinforces their sense of being different and confirms a negative self-identity. The article's core claim is that consistently managing the whole class removes the social 'audience' and oxygen that difficult students' behavior depends on, causing them to fall in line with the classroom's culture instead. He describes this as restoring a healthier, humbler sense of self-worth rather than an inflated or fragile one. The piece closes urging teachers to discard manipulative individualized strategies and instead build general expertise in sound classroom management principles.
points: Fixating on individualized strategies for difficult students while ignoring minor misbehavior from others reinforces the difficult student's negative self-identity.
Consistently managing behavior across the whole class removes the 'audience' that fuels a difficult student's acting out.
When difficult students see everyone else behaving and no one amused by their antics, they tend to conform to classroom culture.
The goal is a humble, realistic sense of self-worth in difficult students, not an inflated or fragile one.
Discard contracts, bribes, and manipulative individualized strategies in favor of general classroom management expertise applied consistently to everyone.
quotes: They try this approach, then that one. They powwow again and again with colleagues and counselors, parents and psychologists.
The problem with this tendency is that ignoring any misbehavior—no matter how innocuous—is lighter fluid for your most difficult students.
It tells them that they are indeed not like the others, that being a behavior problem is who they are and therefore expected. It’s a prophecy they’re quick to fulfill.
But one of the trade secrets to handling difficult students is to focus on managing all students .
You take away their oxygen. You empty the audience from the theater. You leave them alone on stage with no one to perform for.
They experience the dignity of being treated like everyone else . . . and they start behaving like everyone else.
